opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. HED was really one of the first projects I did as a PhD student at UC San Diego, working with my advisor Zhuowen Tu, around 2014 and 2015. It changed how I think about deep learning in a few ways.

Before that, edge detection was a very classical vision problem. People had decades of carefully hand-designed features: gradients, filter banks, texture cues, and then things like structured forests on top. There was a strong sense that you needed a lot of domain knowledge about what an edge "is." What surprised me was that if you took a network pretrained on ImageNet classification, which on the surface has nothing to do with edges, and set up the learning problem in the right way, it could beat all those carefully engineered pipelines by a large margin. That was my first real experience of the idea that representation learning generalizes much further than you'd expect, and that the hard part is often designing the objective and the structure, not the features.

The second lesson was about hierarchy. The core idea in HED was to attach side outputs at different layers of the network and supervise them directly, building on the deeply supervised nets work Zhuowen's group had done. The shallow layers give you fine, precise but noisy edges, and the deeper layers give you coarse but semantically meaningful boundaries. Then you fuse them. Seeing those side outputs visualized was very intuitive: you could literally watch the network move from local, low-level signals to more object-level understanding as you went deeper. It made the idea of a learned multi-scale hierarchy feel concrete rather than abstract. A lot of what later became standard, like feature pyramids and dense prediction with multi-level features, shares that spirit.

The third thing, which matters more to me now looking back, is "holistic," the word in the title. We wanted image-to-image prediction, the whole image in, the whole edge map out, end to end, instead of classifying patches one by one. At the time that felt like a modest engineering choice, but it pointed to a broader belief I've kept: you should let the model see the full context and learn the problem end to end, and avoid breaking it into hand-crafted pieces if you can.

So for me, HED was the moment I really bought into deep learning, not just as a better classifier but as a general way of building vision systems. It also taught me to value simple ideas. The method itself isn't complicated, and I think that's part of why people kept using it. That preference for simple, general designs has stayed with me through later work like ResNeXt and beyond.

r001.rationale: The response describes a learned hierarchy from local, low-level signals in shallow layers to object-level understanding in deeper layers.

r002.rationale: It says shallow layers produce fine, precise edges and deeper layers produce coarser boundaries, the reverse of the criterion.

r003.rationale: It says predictions from different layers are fused, but does not state that this makes the result closer to human understanding of edges.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. HED was actually my first real deep learning project, back around 2014 when I was a PhD student at UCSD with Zhuowen Tu. And honestly, it changed almost everything about how I thought about the field.

Before that, I had come up through a more classical computer vision training. Edge detection was this very old, very well-studied problem, going back to Canny and even earlier. The state of the art at the time was things like Structured Edges from Piotr Dollár, which used random forests on hand-designed features. People had spent decades on it. So the natural question for me was whether a neural network could even compete on something so mature, let alone surpass it.

What we found was that a fully convolutional network, trained end to end with supervision at multiple layers, could just blow past everything. That was a surprise to me. And a few lessons came out of it that I've carried ever since.

The first was about representation. Edges are inherently multi-scale. A boundary of an object and a boundary of a texture live at very different levels of abstraction. In HED, we added side outputs at every stage of the network and supervised them all, and then fused them. What that taught me is that the hierarchy inside a deep network isn't just an implementation detail. The intermediate layers are actually meaningful representations in their own right, and if you design around that hierarchy, you get much better results. That idea stayed with me through ResNeXt and later ConvNeXt, where a lot of the thinking was about how to structure the stages of a network.

The second lesson was about the power of end-to-end learning over hand-designed pipelines. Before HED, people would do feature extraction, then classification, then some post-processing like non-maximum suppression. We showed you could learn most of that holistically, which is where the name comes from. The network learns features, learns the multi-scale fusion, all in one shot. That convinced me that deep learning wasn't just a better classifier bolted onto old pipelines. It was a fundamentally different way of building vision systems.

The third thing, and this is more personal, is that it taught me to trust simple ideas. HED is not a complicated method. Take a pretrained VGG, add side outputs, use a class-balanced loss because edges are very sparse, and train it. A lot of the best work I've been involved in since has that flavor. You find the right simple thing and you do it carefully.

And it also gave me a healthy respect for data and supervision. Edge annotation is very noisy, different annotators disagree a lot. Dealing with that forced me to think about what the model is actually learning from, which became even more important later when I moved toward self-supervised and generative work.

So in short, HED took me from being someone who viewed deep learning as one tool among many to someone who saw it as the organizing principle for how vision should be done. Everything after that, for me, was really building on that shift.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate layers are meaningful and describes a hierarchy inside the network, but does not state that those representations encode a hierarchical structure of the world.

r002.rationale: It describes edges as multi-scale and says HED used side outputs at each stage, but does not say predictions become more detailed from lower to higher layers.

r003.rationale: It says predictions from multiple stages were fused and that this improved results, but does not connect the fusion to an output closer to human understanding of edges.

astra-6.text:
Working on Holistic Edge Detection changed how I thought about representation learning. Edge detection sounds like a very local problem: you look for a change in intensity. But a meaningful boundary often requires understanding the larger image. A texture can produce lots of strong edges, while the boundary of an object can be quite subtle.

That made the hierarchy in a deep network especially interesting to me. Different layers could contribute different kinds of information—fine spatial detail at one level, broader context at another. The question became how to train those levels together and combine them into a useful prediction.

For me, the bigger lesson was that deep learning wasn’t simply replacing a handcrafted feature with a learned feature. It was a way to learn representations jointly with the task. And the architecture and supervision mattered: you had to give the network a structure that helped it learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes layers contributing different kinds of information, but does not say intermediate representations encode a hierarchical structure of the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions fine detail at one level and broader context at another, but does not state that edge predictions become more detailed from lower to higher layers.

r003.rationale: It says layer information can be combined into a useful prediction, but does not connect that output to human understanding of edges.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on Holistic Edge Detection changed how I thought about the representations inside a neural network. Edge detection sounds like a very local problem—you look for changes in color or intensity—but deciding which edges matter also requires a broader understanding of the image. A texture boundary and the outline of an object can look similar locally.

That made the different levels of the network especially interesting to me. Earlier layers preserve fine spatial detail, while deeper layers bring in more context. With HED, we could supervise predictions at multiple stages and combine them, rather than treating everything before the final output as a black box.

For me, the lesson was that deep learning isn’t just about making a network deeper. It’s about understanding how the structure of the task connects to the structure of the model, and how you guide learning along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes different layers as preserving detail or adding context, but does not state that intermediate representations encode a hierarchical structure of the world.

r002.rationale: It says earlier layers preserve fine detail and deeper layers bring context; it does not say edge predictions become more detailed from lower to higher layers.

r003.rationale: It says predictions from multiple stages can be combined, but does not connect that fusion to an output closer to human understanding of edges.
